title: Housecall Pro API Keys and Limits for Developers
summary: Housecall Pro API eligibility depends on your subscription plan and partner status. Confirm whether you can use the API before integrating it.
body_markdown:
## Calling Housecall Pro without code using Activepieces


Without writing a service, you can reach the same Housecall Pro endpoints through Activepieces. Someone still has to own the flow, because when it fails at 2am the person paged is whoever holds the account, not the tool.


Deduplicating events is code you may now have to place inside a flow, and the same discipline applies: decide who owns it before you build it.


### Use the connector for common actions


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/is-activepieces-free-automation-plans-and-limits) chains a trigger to one or more actions, and it has no per-run step charge: a run is 1 credit however many steps it has. Check its Housecall Pro connector first.


If the trigger or action you need appears there, use it: the connector handles the request details, so you have less to maintain and fewer places for a header to go wrong.


Read the connector's action list rather than assuming coverage.


If an endpoint you need is absent, that's a gap in the connector, not proof the API lacks it, and you don't have to wait on a vendor release to close it: Activepieces lets you generate the missing integration with AI and add it privately to your own instance.


**About 60% of its 750 integrations** , counted from the open-source monorepo, were contributed by the community, so the platform's ecosystem grew beyond what the company alone could have built. The Housecall Pro docs remain the authority on what exists.


### Use the HTTP step for the rest


When the connector doesn't cover your action, add an HTTP step and send the same request you verified earlier: the same URL and the same authorization header.


Connections in Activepieces are held centrally and reused across flows, and the run history shows which step failed, so a failing call is something you can inspect rather than guess at.


Keep the credential in the flow's stored connection or secret field, not pasted into the step text, so whoever inherits the flow can't read it off the screen.


### Build a Housecall Pro job-to-Google Sheets workflow


In the flow below, a new Housecall Pro job is written as one row in a Google Sheet, with the HTTP step carrying the authentication header between them.


It shows three stages with nothing hidden between them: an event arrives, a request authenticates, a row lands. Take from it that any failure belongs to exactly one stage, which tells you where to look first. Once it runs, the next step is Monday's work:


1. Name an owner for the flow and a place where its failures are sent.
2. Run one test job and confirm the row appears.
3. Check the flow's run history for errors before trusting it.


For heavy volume, unusual endpoints, or logic the flow builder can't express, custom API calls remain the better choice. For a simple job log, though, this route is enough.
